posts.cooked:
I've looked into things, and it looks like the 100% solution I wanted will be a bigger pain in the butt than I anticipated.  Here are the issues and my proposed plan:

1) My icons aren't really icons.  In the case of the "SV" and "EV" icons, they're just the letters "SV" or "EV" alongside the letter "c" using the Webdings font ("c" displays as a hollow box), with the kerning between the two parts adjusted so that they overlap, making it look like it's a single icon of letters inside a box.  This works well because it allows me to have the "icon" be in-line with the rest of the text, so that as I adjust the text, the "icon" adjusts along with everything else.  If I used an image for the icon instead, every time I adjusted the text a little, I'd have to manually change things so the text flowed properly around the image, which would be a lot of extra work.

2) Why is this a problem?  Because if you click that link for the Webdings font, you'll see that for jeebus-only-knows-why reason, there is a hollow-box webding but not a hollow-circle webding, and certainly no hollow-hexagon.  It's the same for the Symbols font and every other font that I have that uses symbols.  That means unless I want to do a TON of extra work (spoiler: I don't), we're stuck with using the same box shape for "start" and "end".  No stop signs for "stop" and no circles for "start".

3) There are other symbols in that Webdings chart that I could use instead of the hollow-box, and I played around with a couple.  The one that interested me the most was the jaggy speech bubble symbol that maps to the "}" key (very comixy).  However, every one I tried, most especially the jaggy speech bubble, looked too cartoony in the end, and I decided I preferred the simplicity of the box.

So the upshot is what you see in the attached image.  All I'm planning on doing is swapping the colors, making "start" green and "end" red.  Please think that over, and if that won't be enough to make you want to use the villain cards, then there's no point in me even putting in that much effort, and I'll just leave things as they are now.

posts.name: Envisioner
posts.cooked:
jffdougan:

Any chance of doing a supplemental AA table that summarizes which songs are melodies, harmonies, rhythms?

Here's how I memorize them:

  • Harmonies have the most powerful Perform effects - "you or anyone else may play a card", "you or anyone else may use a power", and "blow up any non-character card at the cost of an Instrument" (the latter is not necessarily always useful, but "powerful" certainly fits, given that it can one-shot things up to and including Gloomweaver's 25-HP relics).  Not coincidentally, they are the hardest to Perform - only two of the six Instruments (both of them stringed, if that makes it easier to remember) can activate one of these effects plus an Accompany…of these, only the Harp can Accompany the same card it Performs, which can be important on turn 2 or if you have poor luck acquiring Songs.

  • Melodies have only Perform effects, not Accompanies.  Three Instruments can Perform a Melody, one of them being able to do two at once, and another being able to Accompany a Rhythm first (otherwise, Accompanies always happen second).  Keep in mind that songs are not Limited, so using Drake's Pipes to play two Rhapsodies of Vigor or two Scherzos of Frost and Flame can be highly impressive under the right circumstances (it's a rare day when AA ends up being the party's primary damage dealer, but it can happen).

  • Rhythms can loosely be categorized as the weakest set of songs, with one exception - the single best Accompany under average circumstances belongs to Inventive Preparation.  With an ideal chain setup, you may be able to get several instances of this Accompany, letting your allies play a blitz of extra cards…however, outside of Cloud Cuckooland, Rhythms are generally less likely to have a powerful, instant effect than the other songs (Rhapsody of Vigor is also kind of weak, but it can definitely save your bacon in some games, and we've already mentioned Cedistic Dissonant's extreme-if-highly-situational potency).  Instead, they tend to eke out incremental advantages over time.  If you have Xu's Bell in your hand, you probably want to play a Rhythm, as it's the only Instrument which can Perform a Rhythm (you can always Vocalize them of course, but then that's your whole Power phase, unless you chain into it with one of the two best Harmonies).  Uniquely, the Bell also gives you the ability to Accompany any card which has an Accompany text…it's among no less than four three Instruments which offer access to Rhythm Accompanies, so handing out extra card draws, card plays, and bits of sonic damage is fairly easy to do once or even several times during your turn, if you have a Rhythm and any Instrument other than the Pipes or Harp (you can regard these all as percussion instruments, if you imagine that AA occasionally thumps the Lyra on the side like a drum, instead of or in addition to strumming the strings to Harmonize).

Now, what AA could do if he had a piano, we can only speculate…
